sentences.text: Participant A stated the meeting is the second one and admitted they might be disorganized.
Participant A reported that the previous meeting decided on a universal control handset for all TV video equipment.
Participant A stated the previous decision emphasized that the product must be accessible to a wide range of consumers and ages without limiting anyone.
Participant A stated the previous decision required the product to reflect the company's image, specifically putting 'fashion in electronics'.
Participant A stated the previous decision acknowledged a potential dissonance between the desired product image (uncluttered, undaunting) and the actual budget.
Participant A stated the previous meeting discussed a flip-open design and reducing the size of the control and electronic panel.
Participant B requested to postpone the marketing presentation until later to access more information.
Participant A agreed to postpone the marketing presentation.
Participant D stated they would present first and described the device as one that sends signals to a TV to change its state (power, channel, volume, etc.).
Participant D stated they researched other remote controls and found most use infrared to send signals, likely due to cost, and are powered by batteries.
Participant D noted that most existing remote controls are chunky because they must fit triple A batteries.
Participant D stated that most remote controls have a wireless range of up to about five metres.
Participant D proposed looking at a smaller design and suggested an anti-theft mechanism (like a strap) to prevent the device from being lost.
Participant B confirmed that the anti-theft point was also found in their market research findings.
Participant C attempted to press function F8 on the laptop, which did not work.
Participant C stated that their method involves brainstorming from the last meeting, developing valuable points, and seeking feedback from marketing due to a lack of marketing data
Participant C proposed simplifying interaction with the TV to make it user-friendly by reducing complex buttons, suggesting a flip-top model where main functions are on top and the
Participant C suggested that the flip-top model should allow the trendy generation to program favorite channels in the middle part, accessible to a wide range of audience, and add
Participant C proposed a shock-proof body design to appeal to many people
Participant C noted that most people prefer user-friendly remote controls over complex ones, citing that 30% to 40% of users do not use most buttons
Participant C suggested going for economies of scale by 50 million to add more features and make the product less costly
Participant C suggested looking at whether buttons should be soft or hard, noting that buttons tend to feel hard after continuous use
Participant C summarized the overall design approach as simple and user-friendly
Participant B stated that the company used the company's usability lab to conduct market research with a cross-section of the general public (male and female, ages 15 upwards) and
Participant B reported that 100 subjects were observed in the lab regarding their general use of the remote control
Participant B reported that 75% of users find most remote controls ugly and 80% would spend more money if a remote control looked fancy
Participant B reported that 75% of users zap a lot (channel hopping)
Participant B reported that 50% of users only use 10% of the buttons
Participant B reported that 50% of users are frustrated that remote controls are often lost or slip down the back of the sofa
Participant B reported that 34% of people take too much time to learn to use the remote control
Participant B reported that slightly more than a quarter of people said repetitive strain injury (shoulder and elbow problems) is bad due to small movements of the remote control
Participant B reported that the vast majority of the 35 and under age group would like a liquid crystal display (LCD) and speech recognition features
Participant B reported that the preference for LCD and speech recognition reverses in the 35 to 45 and older age groups
Participant B offered to email extra details if more information is needed
Participant A stated that new project requirements indicate consumers consider teletext outdated with the internet
Participant A stated that the control is only going to be for TV and not a combined control, which limits cost and makes it easier to understand for the consumer
Participant B asked if the video recording function could be programmed with the remote control
Participant A stated that the remote control says 'for TV only' and suggested Sky things might be incorporated
Participant B asked if 'TV only' implies video use
Participant A stated that general TV controls do video as well
Participant D agreed that combined TV and video controls exist, such as Sky boxes with plus boxes that can record straight off the TV
Participant A stated that the team assumes the control still has play and stop functions and programming
Participant D suggested that incorporating speech recognition would be quite expensive and the technology is not that great
Participant B reported that the market research table did not differentiate between the two questions regarding LCD screens and speech recognition
Participant B reported that there were substantial 'don't knows' in the older age group regarding new technology, attributing it to general fear
Participant A suggested using a pack on the TV to hide the remote so users cannot see it, allowing them to press a button on top of the TV that beeps to indicate its location.
Participant A proposed that the corporate logo be incorporated into the handset design to make it fashionable and trendy, noting that people pay more for devices that look good.
Participant B stated that further market research is needed to determine what is attractive to different demographics, specifically noting that preferences vary significantly for a
Participant B noted that attractive features will differ between a trendy New Yorker and a retired South African, implying a need for varied designs across international markets.
Participant C asked if the team was discussing a single model or multiple designs, and Participant D confirmed that several different designs could be created.
Participant C clarified that the internal engineering design would remain essentially the same across different designs, while only the body shape and features might vary slightly.
Participant A suggested using big, rubber buttons rather than tiny ones, noting that this might appeal to young office workers in Japan.
Participant A proposed a touch screen panel as an alternative to physical buttons, suggesting it might appeal to young office people in Japan.
Participant B stated that a touch screen design would appeal to certain sections of the market.
Participant A noted that touch screens could be easily labeled to avoid being daunting for older generations.
Participant D cited the Xbox controller example, explaining that Japanese people have smaller hands and would not buy a controller that is physically too big.
Participant D suggested that button sizes could be adjusted for different countries, with bigger buttons for some and smaller ones for others.
Participant C raised the risk of repetitive strain injury (RSI) and suggested that a touch screen might be a better option to mitigate this risk.
Participant B expressed concern that moving fingers around on a small screen does not adequately address the RSI issue, as RSI is caused by repetitive small movements.
Participant B stated that the RSI issue remains a question mark and suggested it might need to be postponed to a future meeting, though they acknowledged it is something the team
Participant D noted that changing channels requires moving the arm, which can become ridiculous if not addressed.
Participant A mentioned speech recognition as an extremely expensive way to avoid the need for physical buttons.
Participant B asked whether the team should initially focus on a younger age group before broadening the market to everyone.
Participant C suggested focusing on the biggest market, specifically noting that people aged 20 to 35 are the largest demographic.
Participant B noted that the team's current ideas automatically focus on business people and young trendy people, whereas baby boomers represent a larger population.
Participant A stated that the team is currently focusing on a mid-range business class type rather than the older generations.
Participant B expressed a concern about budgetary issues and the desire not to be profligate during broad-scale marketing, suggesting they should focus on where the idea will be
Participant A suggested using the 'Video Plus' function (a 5 or 6-digit code) as an alternative to programming, noting it is easy to use and records programs based on a number code
Participant A explained that the Video Plus code system allows users to record programs by entering a number without needing to specify dates, times, or channels.
Participant D confirmed that the Video Plus function is well known and has been around for a long time, though it is not very well advertised.
Participant B noted that Sky allows users to record programs by clicking a button once for a single episode or twice for a whole series.
Participant D agreed that having the Video Plus function would be really good.
Participant B suggested that retail outlets could offer a similar service to companies like Carphone Warehouse, allowing older users to pop in for help if they are deterred from
Participant D stated that the only problem with offering in-store help for mobile phones is that users have signed contracts with companies that have an obligation to help them,
Participant A suggested using instruction manuals and a customer service phone number to avoid call-out charges and the need to visit a physical shop.
Participant C noted that walking down the street might be too much effort for some users, though they agreed remote users would likely refer to the manual.
Participant B stated the focus is on simple functions, noting that people often put manuals in drawers until something goes wrong, at which point they try to search through them.
Participant A proposed a concept for a rechargeable remote with a docking station to reduce size and eliminate the need to buy batteries repeatedly.
Participant A and Participant D discussed using a rechargeable battery similar to mobile phone batteries that can be charged at night or when not in use.
Participant A expressed a concern that a 'big box' design with many things could cause repetitive strain injury, regardless of how simple it is made.
Participant B noted that many remote controls look identical (brown rectangles with same-colored buttons) and suggested avoiding this look.
Participant C described a design concept involving a flat, box-like shape (like a chocolate) that curls up into a banana or boat shape to reduce thumb strain.
Participant C suggested the bottom of the remote could be moulded to the hand in a semi-circular or smooth shape.
Participant A proposed incorporating the company logo into the design, such as a vague 'C' shape that opens like a shell.
Participant B suggested looking at mobile phone designs to incorporate a logo in the corner of the model rather than making the entire remote look like a sea shell.
Participant B proposed that a lightweight plastic remote with a conch or scallop shell exterior could serve as an ornament, reducing the risk of it being lost.
Participant C suggested considering five or six different designs to choose the most appealing one as the common design.
Participant B reviewed new project requirements, confirming the remote is for TV/video only (not teletext) and that the corporate image (videoplus) should be incorporated.
Participant B explained that the 'videoplus' feature replaces the date and channel programming buttons, serving as an advertisement feature with a reminder to check the guide.
Participant A confirmed that the instruction manual should be simple, different from existing ones, and include a reminder about using videoplus.
Participant A mentioned a potential need for an alarm or beeping function to help with detection if the device is lost.
Participant B asked what specific marketing tasks were needed before the next meeting.
Participant A suggested looking into instruction manuals, noting that people often have a pile of them but rarely use them.
Participant B mentioned a 'questionnaire four' as a potential task.
Participant A offered to email any remaining questions and wait until everyone is connected before answering.
Participant A stated that the meeting is a conceptual design discussion regarding properties, materials, user interface, and trend watching.
Participant A noted that the team is slightly ahead of schedule compared to the last meeting.
Participant A reported that the team decided to leave out voice recognition.
Participant A reported that the team decided on a flip design.
Participant A reported that the team decided on a different shape from the normal shell design.
Participant A stated that the team was going to look into rechargeable batteries.
Participant A stated that the team was going to think about the port and an alarm for getting the device lost.
Participant A stated that the original market plan was a young business kind of range.
Participant B presented feedback from the marketing department indicating that the most important aspect for remote controls is a 'fancy look and feel,' which is twice as important
Participant B stated that 'technologically innovative' is the second most important aspect, twice as important as 'easy to use.'
Participant B reported that market research with 100 subjects found that people want a fancy look and feel rather than the current functional look and feel.
Participant B stated that consultants in Paris and Milan found that fruit and vegetables are the theme for clothes, shoes, and furniture.
Participant B reported a trend towards a spongy feel in materials, contrasting with last year.
Participant D identified the chip used in most TV remotes as the 't.a. double one eight three five.'
Participant D stated that there is no rechargeable battery option available.
Participant D stated that standard double A and triple A batteries were considered too bulky.
Participant D described dynamo charging as similar to a wind-up radio.
Participant D stated that dynamo charging would require a physical handle to wind up.
Participant D stated that kinetic charging is like wristwatches and charges through movement without the user needing to actively shake it.
Participant D stated that a kinetic battery would be a smaller cell similar to a watch battery.
Participant D stated that they have never seen a kinetic watch battery run out overnight.
Participant A questioned whether kinetic charging would be sufficient given that the device is only used for an incredibly short amount of time to send a signal.
Participant B asked if solar charging is compatible with standard batteries, specifically if users could use standard batteries while also utilizing solar charging.
Participant D suggested a dual power option where solar cells would need to be placed on the case, noting that solar cells are quite large and identical in appearance, which would
Participant C stated that solar charging would be slightly expensive, and Participant A agreed that it would also be expensive.
Participant C provided a price estimate of twelve point f (12.0) for normal batteries.
Participant D noted that normal batteries are the cheapest option but expressed concern that solar charging components are not very resistant to dropping, as remotes are frequently
Participant D explained that calculators have smaller batteries and do not get thrown around as much as remotes, which are subject to significant wear.
Participant C asked which battery type would last the longest to prevent customers from needing to charge the device daily like a mobile phone.
Participant D stated that adding solar charging alongside standard batteries would detract from the attractiveness of the feature and add nothing of value.
Participant A proposed adding an attachment to the closing feature, noting that if the device is small, portable, and shaped differently (kinetic), it would be less likely to be
Participant D agreed that the kinetic feature would reduce the risk of losing the device.
Participant D noted that the idea of an attachment for the closing feature did not appear in any focus groups or market research and is not something customers are currently
Participant D explained that current remotes use a silicone printed circuit board (PCB) with closely spaced contacts that connect the circuit when the rubber button is pressed.
Participant D stated that the printed circuit board can be printed to be as big or as small as required, allowing for a much smaller switch design by placing tracks virtually right
Participant D mentioned an option to use an array of switches, which they intended to discuss in the next part of their findings.
Participant D proposed that to conserve battery life, the remote should be in a standby mode when not in use, noting that some devices have lights behind buttons that are more
Participant D suggested that if buttons with lights were chosen, the lights could be turned off after five or ten seconds of non-use.
Participant D discussed case materials, noting that while wood is an option, titanium is very expensive to process and rubber might be considered to provide a spongy feel that some
Participant D explained that the buttons are currently made from material used in stress ball manufacture, which is meant to be anti-slip.
Participant D noted that titanium cases are restricted to a standard box shape by the factory, whereas plastic cases can be made in curved shapes.
Participant C asked if the feature of changing the cover color (like a 'skin' for a flip phone) is available in titanium or only specific to plastic.
Participant D stated that the color-changing cover feature is not available in titanium because it would be too expensive to buy a new case for it.
Participant D noted that titanium is light and strong but should be reserved for aircraft design rather than for a remote, and that it marks quite easily if dropped.
Participant B proposed making the basic mould out of plastic with a removable rubber cover to achieve a spongy feel and allow for different fascia colors.
Participant A clarified that instead of the plastic fascia coming off, the rubber fascia would be the removable component, similar to grip sleeves on pens.
Participant C agreed that the removable rubber fascia idea would be comfortable to hold and could be a good solution.
Participant B noted that the removable rubber fascia would be a very cheap way to change the look of the device, allowing customers to buy a new one if desired.
Participant D mentioned a plan to do some sort of touch screen interface.
Participant D proposed two options for the interface: a bare PCB that could be printed in different colors to make connections via touch, or an LCD screen.
Participant D suggested that if the device had a shell that opened, the interior could be a flat screen with touch buttons or rubber buttons made of anti-slip material.
Participant A noted that having a contrast between the rubber exterior and a fancy-looking interior would be good.
Participant A raised a concern that it would be difficult to distinguish where to press if the device was bare without distinct buttons.
Participant D admitted they had not really thought of how to distinguish where to press on a bare device.
Participant B suggested an option where users could use their fingers to press buttons or use a small pointer/stylus.
Participant D suggested a retractable stylus but noted it might be easily lost, citing a 'palm pop' as an example.
Participant C stated that users who frequently switch channels or use specific functions might find using a pointer irritating and could spoil the touch pad quickly compared to a.
Participant B suggested that users might not actually need a pointer and could use a pencil or pen instead.
Participant A proposed that the meeting should continue with other topics before returning to the pointer issue.
Participant C proposed customizing two circuits for different types of buttons, keeping standard buttons on the top and more complex buttons under the flip top.
Participant D agreed that having two separate circuit boards joined by wires or cabling would be fairly simple.
Participant B suggested a feature where a flip-top shell acts as a compact mirror that responds to body movement, displaying an advertising screen when turned away.
Participant A noted that the marketing team targets both men and women.
Participant A suggested that users might open the device to check their appearance (e.g., before showering or doing hair) while watching TV.
Participant B dismissed the mirror idea as just a quick passing thought.
Participant C shared that the design team checked customer needs and feasibility from previous meetings, noting competitors offer little variety and people are bored of black and白色
Participant C observed that competitor designs are generally rectangular, monotonous, and lack variety.
Participant C noted that there is too much confusion among competitors, with no particular remote being standard.
Participant C explained that the only common feature across competitor remotes is channel and volume control, while other buttons are disorganized and inconsistent.
Participant C proposed incorporating a Graphic User Interface (GUI) in the middle of the flip top, using icons on the LCD screen to simplify operation.
Participant C proposed a combination of boards: a simpler board on the top for standard buttons and a more complex board under the flip top.
Participant A suggested swapping the button placement so frequently used buttons are on the bottom part, as users would use their thumbs to press them like a mobile phone.
Participant B clarified that if the device is flipped open, the user holds it in the palm of their hand with the LCD display and buttons accessible.
Participant A proposed having volume and program controls on the lower side of the device.
Participant C confirmed that volume and channel control buttons are currently repetitive and confusing, and proposed keeping a standardized central pattern for these features as it
Participant C proposed incorporating a voice recognition feature where the remote answers 'I am here' or makes a bleep sound.
Participant C stated that the marketing department wants the design to be trendy and technologically innovative, suggesting inspiration from fruit colors like red chili or tomato.
Participant C proposed keeping the standard central pattern for volume and channel controls as it is the most consistent feature across all models.
Participant A stated they were not sure how much time was left but needed to make a decision on the discussed topics.
Participant B stated that the group had decided on kinetic charging.
Participant B noted that the decision regarding double A or triple A batteries was made because the kinetic batteries still require charging in that manner.
Participant D explained that the kinetic batteries come with a watch-type battery that is smaller.
Participant A confirmed that the internal battery components are standardised across the board.
Participant D stated that the top side of the flip screen will use an LCD display.
Participant D stated that the bottom side of the flip screen will use rubberised buttons.
Participant B requested a repeat of the previous point regarding the button types.
Participant D clarified that the top side will have an LCD and the bottom side will have rubberised buttons.
Participant C suggested using plastic for the body design.
Participant C suggested using rubber for padding or grip to add to the design.
Participant B stated the group decided on a rubber casing for the plastic shell with a variety of designs.
Participant B stated the group will use vegetable and fruit colours for the rubber cover but will not attempt to make the shell itself look like a vegetable or fruit.
Participant A stated the material would be cheap.
Participant A suggested the design could be red, psychedelic, or black and white zebra stripes.
Participant B stated the focus is on the feel of the device.
Participant B stated that market research indicated people wanted a 'fancy look and feel'.
Participant A suggested the design could be clean looking, beige and black.
Participant A suggested the design could contrast with the market, similar to talking-point clocks.
Participant B stated that the rubberised covers are relatively cheap to produce.
Participant B suggested that if feedback from design fairs shows something else is coming in a year's time, the group can easily produce different options like rubbery spikes.
Participant C suggested incorporating acupressure points into the design.
Participant C stated that the body should be moulded in such a way that the case or casing can be changed.
Participant D clarified that the changeable part should be the rubber thing that goes round the outside, not the actual plastic outside case.
Participant C stated the group will incorporate the company logo into the design.
Participant B stated that the logo needs to be obvious so it is clear the product is theirs.
Participant A stated that associating the name with the individual product addresses the need for the logo to stand out.
Participant B confirmed that the group discussed a beeper for location tracking at the last meeting.
Participant A stated that the group is looking into a beeper for location tracking via a company memo.
Participant D stated that the company has the beeper in stock.
Participant A stated that if the beeper turns out to be hugely expensive, the group would have to cut costs elsewhere.
Participant B proposed using a seven-point scale (1 = true, 7 = false) to evaluate the prototype against criteria, with the option to collect individual ratings and calculate an平均.
Participant B rated the prototype's 'fancy look and feel' as a 2, while Participants D, A, and C rated it as 3, 2, and 4 respectively, resulting in an average of 2.75.
Participant B rated the prototype's 'technologically innovative' aspect as a 3, while Participants D and A rated it as 1 and 2 respectively.
Participant C initially rated the 'fancy look and feel' as a 4 but corrected their rating to a 2 after realizing they had entered it incorrectly.
Participant B stated that the team is currently evaluating the prototype to determine if it meets the criteria established in previous market research meetings.
The evaluation criteria identified include: a fancy look and feel, technological innovation, ease of use, incorporation of current fashion trends (specifically spongy texture and '
The team remained slightly ambivalent about using voice recognition, though it was noted as the favoured strategy, with a beeper function considered as an alternative.
Participant B proposed that the team would discuss each criterion individually and reach a consensus rating between 1 and 7.
Participant B mentioned that the prototype design includes a clamshell structure with a plastic body, a rubberized outer casing, and a top LCD screen.
The team decided to use infrared transmission for the remote control, placing the sender on the front of the bottom layer.
The team decided to incorporate a company logo on the inside of the product, either as a bezzled logo, an inset, or an engraving, ensuring it does not interfere with the outside.
Participant A confirmed they have evaluation criteria to present.
Participant B stated that the current stage of evaluation is for the team to assess if the product specification and prototype design meet the criteria from market research.
Participant C confirmed that the evaluation process involves looking at specific criteria such as 'fancy look and feel' and 'technologically innovative'.
Participant B mentioned that the team is waiting for Participant F's rating to complete the calculation for the 'technologically innovative' criterion.
Participants A, B, and C agreed on the use of a kinetic battery.
